docs.title: flapsim.robot.manifest
docs.text:
Robot manifest: what a URDF or MJCF file cannot say about a flapping robot.

A manifest is a small YAML or JSON document that lives next to the model file. It names the torso and the wings, gives each wing its aerodynamic frame, its stroke and feathering joints and its planform, and lists the model patches (joint dynamics, equality constraints, mass overrides) that MuJoCo needs but URDF cannot express. :meth:RobotManifest.from_file parses and validates it and :func:flapsim.robot.load turns it into a compiled MuJoCo model with :class:~flapsim.wings.Wing objects attached.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Vectors are expressed in the frame of the body they belong to.
  • frame.span points from the wing root to the tip along the feathering axis; frame.chord points from the leading edge (the hinge line) to the trailing edge. FlapSim derives the surface normal from them, so the side of the hinge on which the wing lies is never ambiguous.
  • sign on a joint reference converts the MuJoCo joint coordinate into the aerodynamic convention: psi = sign * qpos.
  • when on a patch restricts it to "fixed" or "free" base models; the default "always" applies it to both.

docs.title: WingMass dataclass
docs.text:
Mass properties of a wing body, given in wing coordinates.

Wing coordinates are (normal, span, chord) with span positive from root to tip and chord positive from the leading to the trailing edge, so mirrored wings share the same numbers.

  • type: thin_plate: a uniform plate covering length x mean_chord.
  • type: spar_plate: a leading-edge spar (rod along the span) holding spar_fraction of the mass plus a uniform membrane plate holding the rest. This is the usual mass distribution of a membrane wing and the one that gives physically correct passive feathering.
  • type: explicit: com and diaginertia about the wing axes through the centre of mass.

docs.title: Planform dataclass
docs.text:
Wing planform: how to obtain the blade-element integrals.

profile selects the source: an analytic shape (rectangular or elliptic, needs length and mean_chord), a chord polyline of (r, c) pairs in metres from root to tip, or explicit integrals. pitch_axis_fraction is the chordwise position of the feathering axis measured from the leading edge as a fraction of the chord (hinge inside the plate); leading_edge_offset is the distance in metres from the feathering axis to the leading edge when the plate starts beyond the hinge (a root spar). Use one or the other.

docs.text:
A two-wing flapper with rectangular flat-plate wings.

The torso sits at the origin and the wings span the body x axis. At the neutral pose each plate is vertical: its normal points along -y (the stroke direction) and its chord hangs down (-z) from the leading-edge hinge. This is the quasi-steady model's convention, in which a feathering angle of zero means the plate meets the stroke flow at 90 degrees. The stroke joints rotate about +z (left) and -z (right), so equal joint angles give mirrored motion; the passive feathering joints rotate about +x for both wings. Returns the MjSpec and a matching manifest; pass both to :func:flapsim.robot.load. The wing mass is distributed as a leading-edge spar (spar_fraction) plus a membrane plate through the manifest's mass model.

docs.text:
Runtime wing: a manifest :class:WingSpec resolved against a MuJoCo model.

The aerodynamic frame of a wing has +X along the surface normal, +Y along the feathering axis and +Z = X x Y; the chord extends from the hinge along -Z. From the manifest's span (root to tip) and chord (leading to trailing edge) vectors: Y = side * span, Z = -chord and X = Y x Z. Mirrored wings therefore share one frame orientation at the neutral pose (for a right wing +Y is the negative root-to-tip direction) and the side factor in the aerodynamic formulas puts the centre of pressure back on the wing. This is the convention of the quasi-steady model in :mod:flapsim.fluid.aero.

docs.title: flapsim.wings.planform
docs.text:
Wing planform integrals for blade-element aerodynamics.

The quasi-steady model needs chord-weighted radial moments of the planform. With the non-dimensional span coordinate r_hat = r / R and chord c_hat = c(r) / c_mean they are

  • r_kk = integral c_hat * r_hat**k for k = 0..3 (normal force),
  • z_cpk = integral c_hat**2 * r_hat**k for k = 0..2 (pitching moment),
  • z_rd = integral (|y_te| y_te**3 - |y_le| y_le**3) / c_mean**4 (rotational damping), where y is the chordwise distance from the feathering axis to the trailing and leading edges.

For a rectangular wing hinged at its leading edge all of them are 1 / (k + 1) and z_rd = 1. Several constructors are offered: analytic profiles, a chord polyline, a planform polygon and a mesh outline.

docs.title: Quasi-steady aerodynamic derivation for a flapping-wing robot in ideal hover
docs.text: Translated from the Chinese original (docs/zh/derivations/hover_simplification.md). It documents the implementation as it stood before 2026-10-28; the pitching-moment sign and the removed force flip are described in quasi_steady_model.md.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text:
This document gives a simplified derivation of the flapping-wing aerodynamic model in FlapSim, suitable for the main text of a paper. The object of study is restricted to symmetric hover: the instantaneous translational and angular velocities of the body are zero, the stroke-plane angle and the wing deviation angle are zero, and the main wing motion is described by the stroke angle and the passive feathering angle. Under these conditions the in-plane velocity retains only the stroke velocity, which is proportional to the spanwise coordinate, so the first-order and constant terms of the velocity-squared polynomial both vanish, i.e.

\[ a_{U1}=0,\qquad a_{U0}=0. \]

On this basis the document derives in turn the single-wing normal force, the aerodynamic pitching moment, the centre of pressure, the rotational damping moment, the single-wing wrench in the world frame, and the total lift of the two wings. Finally it states the condition under which the cycle-averaged lift is proportional to the square of the flapping frequency.

docs.title: 1. Model assumptions
docs.text:
To obtain clear closed-form expressions usable in a paper, the following assumptions are adopted.

  1. The body is approximately stationary at the instant of the aerodynamic computation:

$$ \boldsymbol v_B=\boldsymbol 0,\qquad \boldsymbol\omega_B=\boldsymbol 0. $$

  1. The stroke-plane angle and the wing deviation angle are both zero:

$$ \Phi=0,\quad\dot\Phi=0,\qquad \phi=0,\quad\dot\phi=0. $$

  1. The left and right wings have identical geometry and move in mirror symmetry.

  2. The instantaneous angle of attack along the span is approximated by the angle of attack at the representative centre of pressure, i.e. the whole wing uses the same normal-force coefficient at any instant.

  3. The aerodynamic force follows a quasi-steady blade-element model; wake capture, added mass, wing–wing interaction and dynamic stall are not considered explicitly.

  4. The derivation uses the raw, unclipped aerodynamic forces and takes lift_scale = moment_scale = 1. The centre-of-pressure relation \(c_{cp}=-M_{aero}/F_N\) therefore holds exactly.

It must be stressed that \(a_{U1}=a_{U0}=0\) is not an identity of the full six-degree-of-freedom model. It holds only under the ideal-hover assumptions above. When the body translates or rotates, or the stroke plane has an offset motion, these two terms are in general non-zero.

docs.title: 2.1 Coordinate frames
docs.text:
Before reading the formulas that follow, one must distinguish "the components of a vector" from "the actual direction of the vector in the world". This document uses three levels of coordinate frames.

Symbol Frame Definition \(\{W\}\) world frame \(+z_W\) vertically upward \(\{B\}\) body frame fixed to the robot body \(\{A_k\}\) aerodynamic frame of wing \(k\) \(+x_A\) is the wing normal, \(+y_A\) the spanwise/feathering axis, \(-z_A\) points towards the chordwise CoP

The relationship between the frames is shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1 Relationship between the world frame, the body frame and the wing aerodynamic frames.

Here \(k\in\{L,R\}\) denotes the left and right wing respectively. Define

\[ R_{WB}\in SO(3) \]

as the rotation matrix from the body frame to the world frame, and

\[ R_{WA,k}\in SO(3) \]

as the rotation matrix from the aerodynamic frame of wing \(k\) to the world frame. Any wing-local vector \(\boldsymbol q_{A,k}\) transforms to the world frame as

\[ \boldsymbol q_{W,k}=R_{WA,k}\boldsymbol q_{A,k}. \]

If \(R_{BA,k}\) denotes the rotation matrix from the aerodynamic frame to the body frame, the three satisfy

\[ \boxed{ R_{WA,k}=R_{WB}R_{BA,k} }. \]

The coordinate transformation can therefore be understood in two steps:

\[ \{A_k\} \xrightarrow{\ R_{BA,k}\ } \{B\} \xrightarrow{\ R_{WB}\ } \{W\}. \]

In the program, \(R_{WA,k}\) is determined jointly by the MuJoCo wing-body orientation and the fixed alignment matrix from the URDF/STL frame to the aerodynamic frame. The derivation below only needs the final \(R_{WA,k}\).

docs.title: 2.2 Why \(F_N\) is written in the first component
docs.text:
The column vector

\[ \boldsymbol F_{A,k} = \begin{bmatrix} F_{N,k}\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

represents "the three components of the force in the aerodynamic frame \(\{A_k\}\)", in the fixed order

\[ \begin{bmatrix} x_A\text{ component}\\ y_A\text{ component}\\ z_A\text{ component} \end{bmatrix}. \]

So \(F_N\) sits in the first position not because it points along the first world axis, nor because it is the "first row" of some matrix. There is only one reason:

\[ \boxed{ \text{this model defines the wing surface normal as the }+x_A\text{ axis of the aerodynamic frame} }. \]

The normal force acts only along \(+x_A\), so its coordinates in \(\{A_k\}\) are necessarily

\[ \boldsymbol F_{A,k} =F_{N,k}\boldsymbol e_{x_A} =F_{N,k} \begin{bmatrix} 1\\0\\0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

\(F_N\) is a signed scalar: \(F_N>0\) means the force points along \(+x_A\), \(F_N<0\) means it points along \(-x_A\). There is therefore no need to define separate force vectors for the two directions.

Only after this local vector is transformed to the world frame does one obtain the actual spatial direction:

\[ \boldsymbol F_{W,k} =R_{WA,k}\boldsymbol F_{A,k}. \]

Writing the rotation matrix by columns,

\[ R_{WA,k} = \begin{bmatrix} \vert&\vert&\vert\\ \boldsymbol e_{x_A}^{W} &\boldsymbol e_{y_A}^{W} &\boldsymbol e_{z_A}^{W}\\ \vert&\vert&\vert \end{bmatrix}, \]

where \(\boldsymbol e_{x_A}^{W}\) denotes "the wing-local \(+x_A\) unit axis expressed in the world frame". Then

\[ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol F_{W,k} &= \begin{bmatrix} \vert&\vert&\vert\\ \boldsymbol e_{x_A}^{W} &\boldsymbol e_{y_A}^{W} &\boldsymbol e_{z_A}^{W}\\ \vert&\vert&\vert \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} F_{N,k}\\0\\0 \end{bmatrix}\\ &=F_{N,k}\boldsymbol e_{x_A}^{W}. \end{aligned} \]

This shows that multiplying by \([F_N,0,0]^T\) simply selects the first column of \(R_{WA,k}\) and scales it by \(F_N\). Hence:

  • in the wing aerodynamic frame, \(F_N\) is always the first component;
  • in the world frame, \(F_N\) can have all three components \(x_W\), \(y_W\) and \(z_W\) at once;
  • a change of wing attitude changes the world direction of the force through \(R_{WA,k}\), without changing how the local force vector is written.

For example, if at some instant

\[ \boldsymbol e_{x_A}^{W} = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\0\\-1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

then

\[ \boldsymbol F_{W,k} = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\0\\-F_{N,k} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Although \(F_N\) is the first component in local coordinates, in world coordinates it lies entirely along \(-z_W\). The current adapter subsequently also flips the sign of the force according to the STL normal convention, so the force actually applied is \(-\boldsymbol F_{W,k}\).

docs.title: 2.3 Left/right wings and the direction of the centre of pressure
docs.text:
This document uses one common aerodynamic frame convention for both wings and handles the mirror relationship with

\[ s_L=+1,\qquad s_R=-1 \]

The local coordinates of the centre of pressure are therefore

\[ \boxed{ \boldsymbol r_{cp,A,k} = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ s_kr_{cp}\\ -c_{cp,k} \end{bmatrix} }. \]

The three components mean, in order:

  1. the centre of pressure lies in the wing plane, so its normal coordinate is \(0\);
  2. the spanwise positions of the left and right wings are \(+r_{cp}\) and \(-r_{cp}\) respectively;
  3. the chordwise centre of pressure lies along the \(-z_A\) direction defined here, hence it is written \(-c_{cp}\).

docs.title: 2.4 Main symbols
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning Unit \(R\) single-wing span m \(r\) spanwise coordinate, \(0\le r\le R\) m \(c(r)\) local chord m \(\bar c\) mean chord m \(\rho\) air density kg/m³ \(\psi\), \(\dot\psi\) stroke angle and stroke rate rad, rad/s \(\theta\), \(\dot\theta\) feathering angle and feathering rate rad, rad/s \(U_i\) in-plane relative velocity m/s \(U_o\) out-of-plane relative velocity m/s \(\alpha\) instantaneous angle of attack rad \(C_N\) normal-force coefficient — \(F_N\) single-wing local normal force N \(M_{aero}\) aerodynamic pitching moment from the pressure distribution N·m \(M_{rd}\) feathering rotational damping moment N·m \(r_{cp}\) spanwise centre-of-pressure position m \(c_{cp}\) chordwise centre-of-pressure distance m \(s_k\) left/right wing sign, \(s_L=+1,\ s_R=-1\) —

The current rectangular-wing parameters are

\[ R=0.07\ \mathrm m,\qquad \bar c=0.02\ \mathrm m,\qquad \rho=1.225\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}. \]

docs.title: 3. Wing geometric moments
docs.text:
Define the dimensionless spanwise coordinate and the dimensionless chord:

\[ \hat r=\frac{r}{R},\qquad \hat c(\hat r)=\frac{c(R\hat r)}{\bar c}. \]

The mean chord satisfies

\[ \bar c=\frac{1}{R}\int_0^R c(r)\,dr. \]

The radial geometric moments needed for the normal-force integral are defined as

\[ r_{kk}=\int_0^1\hat c(\hat r)\hat r^k\,d\hat r. \]

This document mainly uses

\[ r_{22}=\int_0^1\hat c(\hat r)\hat r^2\,d\hat r, \qquad r_{33}=\int_0^1\hat c(\hat r)\hat r^3\,d\hat r. \]

The aerodynamic pitching moment also needs the chord-squared weighted moment:

\[ z_{cp,2}= \int_0^1\hat c^2(\hat r)\hat r^2\,d\hat r. \]

For a rectangular wing \(\hat c(\hat r)=1\), so

\[ r_{22}=\frac13,\qquad r_{33}=\frac14,\qquad z_{cp,2}=\frac13. \]

docs.title: 4.1 The general velocity polynomial
docs.text:
The full model writes the in-plane and out-of-plane velocities as first-order functions of the spanwise coordinate:

\[ U_i(r)=U_{i1}r+U_{i0}, \qquad U_o(r)=U_{o1}r+U_{o0}. \]

The local velocity squared can therefore be written as

\[ U^2(r)=U_i^2(r)+U_o^2(r) =a_{U2}r^2+a_{U1}r+a_{U0}, \]

where

\[ \begin{aligned} a_{U2}&=U_{i1}^2+U_{o1}^2,\\ a_{U1}&=2(U_{i1}U_{i0}+U_{o1}U_{o0}),\\ a_{U0}&=U_{i0}^2+U_{o0}^2. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: 4.2 Simplification under the hover assumptions
docs.text:
When the body velocity, the body angular velocity, the stroke-plane motion and the deviation motion are all zero, the main velocity at any point on the wing comes from the stroke alone:

\[ U_i(r)=\dot\psi r,\qquad U_o(r)=0. \]

Comparing with the general form gives

\[ U_{i1}=\dot\psi,\qquad U_{i0}=0,\qquad U_{o1}=0,\qquad U_{o0}=0. \]

Therefore

\[ \boxed{ a_{U2}=\dot\psi^2,\qquad a_{U1}=0,\qquad a_{U0}=0 }. \]

The velocity squared finally degenerates to

\[ \boxed{ U^2(r)=\dot\psi^2r^2 }. \]

This expression is the kinematic basis of all the simplified formulas that follow.

docs.title: 5. Angle of attack and aerodynamic coefficients
5.1 Spanwise representative point
docs.text:
In pure stroke motion the local dynamic pressure is proportional to \(r^2\), so the spanwise point of application of the resultant force is

\[ r_{cp} =\frac{\displaystyle\int_0^R r\,c(r)r^2\,dr} {\displaystyle\int_0^R c(r)r^2\,dr} =R\frac{r_{33}}{r_{22}}. \]

For a rectangular wing,

\[ \boxed{ r_{cp}=\frac34R=0.0525\ \mathrm m }. \]

docs.title: 5.2 Instantaneous angle of attack
docs.text:
At the spanwise representative point,

\[ U_i(r_{cp})=\dot\psi r_{cp},\qquad U_o(r_{cp})=0. \]

The inflow deflection angle is therefore zero and the angle of attack simplifies to

\[ \boxed{ \alpha =\theta+\operatorname{sgn}(\dot\psi)\frac{\pi}{2} }. \]

The normal-force coefficient used by the program is

\[ C_N(\alpha) =1.8\sin(2\alpha)\cos\alpha +1.95\sin\alpha -1.5\cos(2\alpha)\sin\alpha. \]

The chordwise centre-of-pressure fraction is

\[ d_{cp}(\alpha) =0.46-0.332\cos\alpha -0.037\cos(3\alpha) -0.013\cos(5\alpha). \]

The two relations above belong to the empirical aerodynamic model. This document adopts them directly and does not derive them from first principles of fluid mechanics. For a formal submission, the original experimental or modelling source of these empirical coefficients should be added here; this document does not fabricate references that have not been verified.

docs.title: 6. Single-wing normal force
docs.text:
The quasi-steady normal force on a spanwise element \(dr\) is

\[ dF_N =\frac12\rho C_N(\alpha)c(r)U^2(r)\,dr. \]

Substituting

\[ U^2(r)=\dot\psi^2r^2 \]

gives

\[ dF_N =\frac12\rho C_N(\alpha)c(r)\dot\psi^2r^2\,dr. \]

Integrating along the span:

\[ \begin{aligned} F_N &=\frac12\rho C_N(\alpha)\dot\psi^2 \int_0^R c(r)r^2\,dr\\ &=\frac12\rho\bar c C_N(\alpha) \dot\psi^2R^3r_{22}. \end{aligned} \]

Hence the single-wing normal force in ideal hover is

\[ \boxed{ F_N =\frac12\rho\bar c R^3r_{22} C_N(\alpha)\dot\psi^2 }. \]

For the current rectangular wing \(r_{22}=1/3\), so

\[ F_N =\frac16\rho\bar c R^3 C_N(\alpha)\dot\psi^2. \]

docs.title: 7. Aerodynamic pitching moment and chordwise centre of pressure
7.1 Aerodynamic pitching moment
docs.text:
Let the distance from the local centre of pressure to the reference edge be \(d_{cp}(\alpha)c(r)\). The pitching moment produced by the elemental normal force is

\[ dM_{aero} =-d_{cp}(\alpha)c(r)\,dF_N. \]

Substituting the elemental normal force and integrating along the span:

\[ \begin{aligned} M_{aero} &=-\frac12\rho C_N(\alpha)d_{cp}(\alpha)\dot\psi^2 \int_0^R c^2(r)r^2\,dr\\ &=-\frac12\rho\bar c^2R^3z_{cp,2} C_N(\alpha)d_{cp}(\alpha)\dot\psi^2. \end{aligned} \]

Hence

\[ \boxed{ M_{aero} =-\frac12\rho\bar c^2R^3z_{cp,2} C_N(\alpha)d_{cp}(\alpha)\dot\psi^2 }. \]

docs.title: 7.2 Equivalent chordwise centre of pressure
docs.text:
The model does not apply \(M_{aero}\) a second time as an independent moment; instead it converts it into the chordwise point of application of the normal force:

\[ c_{cp}=-\frac{M_{aero}}{F_N}. \]

Substituting the \(F_N\) and \(M_{aero}\) obtained above:

\[ \boxed{ c_{cp} =\bar c\,d_{cp}(\alpha) \frac{z_{cp,2}}{r_{22}} }. \]

For a rectangular wing,

\[ z_{cp,2}=r_{22}=\frac13, \]

so one further obtains

\[ \boxed{ c_{cp}=\bar c\,d_{cp}(\alpha) }. \]

This result shows that, for a rectangular wing under the ideal-hover assumptions, the chordwise centre of pressure equals exactly the local chord times the empirical centre-of-pressure fraction.

docs.title: 8. Feathering rotational damping
docs.text:
The passive feathering motion produces a damping moment that opposes the feathering rate:

\[ \boxed{ M_{rd} =-\frac58\rho R\bar c^4z_{rd} |\dot\theta|\dot\theta }. \]

For the current rectangular wing \(z_{rd}=1\). Since

\[ M_{rd}\dot\theta =-\frac58\rho R\bar c^4z_{rd} |\dot\theta|\dot\theta^2 \le0, \]

the rotational damping always dissipates mechanical energy.

\(M_{aero}\) and \(M_{rd}\) play different physical roles:

  • \(M_{aero}\) is implemented implicitly through the chordwise centre of pressure \(c_{cp}\);
  • \(M_{rd}\) is applied as an independent pure moment about the feathering axis.

docs.title: 9. Single-wing aerodynamic force in the world frame
9.1 Force and centre of pressure in the aerodynamic frame
docs.text:
The normal force of wing \(k\) in its aerodynamic frame is

\[ \boldsymbol F_{A,k} = \begin{bmatrix} F_{N,k}\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The position of the centre of pressure relative to the wing-body origin is

\[ \boldsymbol r_{cp,A,k} = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ s_kr_{cp}\\ -c_{cp,k} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Its world coordinates are

\[ \boldsymbol x_{cp,W,k} =\boldsymbol x_{body,W,k} +R_{WA,k}\boldsymbol r_{cp,A,k}. \]

docs.title: 9.2 Force in the world frame
docs.text:
The single-wing normal force transformed to the world frame is

\[ \boxed{ \boldsymbol F_{W,k} =R_{WA,k} \begin{bmatrix} F_{N,k}\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} }. \]

docs.title: 9.3 Moment about the wing centre of mass
docs.text:
The world-frame lever arm from the wing centre of mass to the centre of pressure is

\[ \boldsymbol\ell_{W,k} =\boldsymbol x_{cp,W,k}-\boldsymbol x_{com,W,k}. \]

The moment produced by the normal force at the centre of pressure is

\[ \boldsymbol\tau_{F,W,k} =\boldsymbol\ell_{W,k}\times\boldsymbol F_{W,k}. \]

The rotational damping moment transformed to the world frame is

\[ \boldsymbol\tau_{rd,W,k} =R_{WA,k} \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ M_{rd,k}\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Hence the total single-wing moment is

\[ \boxed{ \boldsymbol\tau_{W,k} =\boldsymbol\tau_{F,W,k} +\boldsymbol\tau_{rd,W,k} }. \]

The complete single-wing wrench is

\[ \boxed{ \boldsymbol w_k = \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol F_{W,k}\\ \boldsymbol\tau_{W,k} \end{bmatrix} }. \]

docs.title: 10. Total lift of the two wings
10.1 Normal correction
docs.text:
The current STL wing normal is opposite to the oriented normal of the aerodynamic model, so the adapter applies one sign correction to the world-frame aerodynamic force:

\[ \boldsymbol F_{applied,k}=-\boldsymbol F_{W,k}. \]

This sign correction belongs to the current URDF/STL coordinate convention, not to the quasi-steady aerodynamic theory itself. [Translator's note: this force flip was removed on 2026-10-28; see quasi_steady_model.md.]

docs.title: 10.2 World-frame resultant of the two wings
docs.text:
The total aerodynamic force applied to the robot by the left and right wings is

\[ \boxed{ \boldsymbol F_{total} =\boldsymbol F_{applied,L} +\boldsymbol F_{applied,R} }. \]

Substituting the single-wing expressions:

\[ \boldsymbol F_{total} =- R_{WA,L} \begin{bmatrix} F_{N,L}\\0\\0 \end{bmatrix} - R_{WA,R} \begin{bmatrix} F_{N,R}\\0\\0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Define the world-frame vertical unit vector

\[ \boldsymbol e_z= \begin{bmatrix} 0\\0\\1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

then the instantaneous total lift is

\[ \boxed{ F_{\mathrm{lift}} =\boldsymbol e_z^T\boldsymbol F_{total} }. \]

Further defining the projection of the normal of wing \(k\) onto the world vertical,

\[ \gamma_k =\boldsymbol e_z^TR_{WA,k} \begin{bmatrix} 1\\0\\0 \end{bmatrix}, \]

one obtains

\[ \boxed{ F_{\mathrm{lift}} =-\gamma_LF_{N,L} -\gamma_RF_{N,R} }. \]

In the fully symmetric state,

\[ F_{N,L}=F_{N,R}=F_N,\qquad \gamma_L=\gamma_R=\gamma, \]

so

\[ \boxed{ F_{\mathrm{lift}}=-2\gamma F_N }. \]

If the current coordinate convention makes the aerodynamic normal of the wings point along world \(-z_W\), then \(\gamma=-1\) and

\[ \boxed{ F_{\mathrm{lift}}=2F_N }. \]

This step completes the coordinate transformation from the local single-wing normal force to the total lift of the two wings.

docs.title: 11. Cycle-averaged lift and the frequency-squared law
docs.text:
Let the stroke angle be

\[ \psi(t)=A\sin(2\pi ft), \]

then

\[ \dot\psi(t)=2\pi fA\cos(2\pi ft). \]

Substituting into the single-wing normal force:

\[ F_N(t) =\frac12\rho\bar cR^3r_{22} C_N[\alpha(t)] (2\pi fA)^2\cos^2(2\pi ft). \]

The cycle-averaged lift of the two wings is defined as

\[ \bar F_{\mathrm{lift}} =\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T F_{\mathrm{lift}}(t)\,dt, \qquad T=\frac1f. \]

Introducing the dimensionless phase

\[ \xi=2\pi ft, \]

gives

\[ \bar F_{\mathrm{lift}} =K_f f^2, \]

where

\[ \boxed{ K_f =-\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \sum_{k\in\{L,R\}} \gamma_k(\xi) \frac12\rho\bar cR^3r_{22} C_N[\alpha_k(\xi)] (2\pi A)^2\cos^2\xi \,d\xi }. \]

Hence, as long as the following dimensionless periodic quantities do not change significantly with frequency,

\[ \theta_k(\xi),\qquad \gamma_k(\xi),\qquad C_N[\alpha_k(\xi)], \]

the cycle-averaged lift satisfies

\[ \boxed{ \bar F_{\mathrm{lift}}\propto f^2 }. \]

FlapSim's cycle-averaged hover model uses

\[ \bar F_{\mathrm{lift}}=k_f f^2, \]

where \(k_f\) is identified from the full fixed-base flapping simulation rather than prescribed directly by the constant-coefficient approximation above.

docs.title: 12. Summary of the derived results
docs.text:
Under ideal-hover conditions the aerodynamic derivation can be summarised in the following seven steps.

  1. Local velocity:

$$ U_i(r)=\dot\psi r,\qquad U_o(r)=0. $$

  1. Velocity-squared coefficients:

$$ a_{U2}=\dot\psi^2,\qquad a_{U1}=a_{U0}=0. $$

  1. Single-wing normal force:

$$ F_N =\frac12\rho\bar cR^3r_{22} C_N(\alpha)\dot\psi^2. $$

  1. Aerodynamic pitching moment:

$$ M_{aero} =-\frac12\rho\bar c^2R^3z_{cp,2} C_N(\alpha)d_{cp}(\alpha)\dot\psi^2. $$

  1. Centre of pressure:

$$ r_{cp}=R\frac{r_{33}}{r_{22}}, \qquad c_{cp} =\bar c\,d_{cp}\frac{z_{cp,2}}{r_{22}}. $$

  1. Single-wing force in the world frame:

$$ \boldsymbol F_{applied,k} =-R_{WA,k} \begin{bmatrix}F_{N,k}\0\0\end{bmatrix}. $$

  1. Total lift of the two wings:

$$ F_{\mathrm{lift}} =-\gamma_LF_{N,L}-\gamma_RF_{N,R}. $$

In the ideal symmetric state with vertical wing normals:

\[ \boxed{ F_{\mathrm{lift}}=2F_N }. \]

docs.title: 13. Range of validity
docs.text:
The formulas in this document are intended for the ideal-hover theoretical derivation in the paper. In the following situations the full velocity model should be restored, and \(a_{U1}\) and \(a_{U0}\) are in general no longer zero:

  1. the body has a significant translational velocity;
  2. the body has roll, pitch or yaw angular velocity;
  3. the stroke-plane angle or the wing deviation angle is non-zero;
  4. the shoulder-offset velocity is not negligible relative to the local inflow;
  5. the study concerns rapid manoeuvres, strongly coupled attitude changes or large-range free flight.

The simplified model in this document is therefore suited to a "hover-state aerodynamic modelling" section of the paper, while the full FlapSim implementation is suited to numerical simulation and validation in non-ideal states.

docs.title: FlapSim aerodynamics (aero): implementation, derivation and validation
docs.text:
Translated from the Chinese original (docs/zh/derivations/quasi_steady_aero.md). It documents the implementation as it stood before 2026-10-28; the pitching-moment sign and the removed force flip are described in quasi_steady_model.md.

This document keeps the complete code-level implementation and validation details. The simplified ideal-hover derivation intended for the main text of the paper is in hover_simplification.md, where \(a_{U1}=a_{U0}=0\) is taken under explicit assumptions.

This document collects the actual implementation in flapsim/fluid at the time of writing (the per-wing engine now lives in flapsim/aero/). Here "aero" is not one model but two models with different purposes:

  1. fix=True: MuJoCoAeroAdapter calls aero.py and computes quasi-steady aerodynamic forces wing by wing at every simulation step;
  2. fix=False: AveragedHoverAero uses the cycle-averaged force and moment identified from a fixed-base frequency sweep.

One of the two is selected in SimCore.__init__; they never run at the same time. Below we first derive the per-wing model in full, then describe the cycle-averaged model and its identification relationships.

docs.title: 1. Files and the runtime call chain
docs.text:
The key files are:

File Role flapsim/fluid/aero.py Pure aerodynamic computation decoupled from MuJoCo: velocities, angle of attack, normal force, centre of pressure and wrench flapsim/fluid/mujoco_adapter.py (now a thin compatibility wrapper around flapsim/aero/base.py, AeroEngine, and the aero/quasi_steady plugin in flapsim/aero/stack.py) Reads state from MjData, handles the left/right wing frames, writes the wrench into xfrc_applied flapsim/fluid/averaged_hover.py (now flapsim/aero/cycle_averaged.py) Cycle-averaged hover model used in free flight flapsim/config/Wing.json Wing geometry integrals, air density and shoulder geometry parameters flapsim/config/AeroOptions.py Runtime parameters: scaling, clipping, stroke-plane angle and deviation angle flapsim/sim_core.py Selects the aero model according to fix and attaches it to the environment flapsim/environment/environment.py (now flapsim/core/simulation.py, class Simulation) Each step: update the controller first, then apply the aerodynamic forces, finally call mujoco.mj_step

The order of operations in each fixed-base simulation step is

\[ \text{controller} \rightarrow \text{joint state} \rightarrow \texttt{MuJoCoAeroAdapter.apply\_forces} \rightarrow \texttt{aero\_step} \rightarrow \texttt{wing\_aero} \rightarrow \texttt{world\_wrench} \rightarrow \texttt{xfrc\_applied} \rightarrow \texttt{mj\_step}. \]

TrajectoryController (now flapsim/actuators/sinusoidal_stroke.py) prescribes the stroke angle as

\[ \psi(t)=dA\sin(2\pi ft+\varphi_0),\qquad \dot\psi(t)=dA(2\pi f)\cos(2\pi ft+\varphi_0), \]

where \(d\in\{-1,+1\}\) is the left/right wing direction and the default amplitude is \(A=1.5\ \mathrm{rad}\).

docs.title: 2.1 Body state
docs.text:
Let \(R_{WB}\) be the rotation matrix from body coordinates to world coordinates. The world-frame velocities given by MuJoCo are first transformed into the body frame:

\[ \boldsymbol v_B=R_{WB}^{T}\boldsymbol v_W=(u,v,w)^T, \qquad \boldsymbol\omega_B=R_{WB}^{T}\boldsymbol\omega_W=(p,q,r)^T. \]

The implementation clips \(\lVert\boldsymbol\omega_B\rVert\) to angular_velocity_limit, default \(5000\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The linear velocity is not clipped in the same way.

docs.title: 2.2 Wing motion variables
docs.text:
• \(s=+1\): left wing; \(s=-1\): right wing;
  • \(\psi,\dot\psi\): stroke angle and stroke rate;
  • \(\theta,\dot\theta\): feathering / wing pitch angle and its rate;
  • \(\phi,\dot\phi\): deviation angle, named deviation_angle/rate in the code;
  • \(\Phi,\dot\Phi\): stroke-plane angle, named stroke_plane_angle/rate in the code;
  • \(d_0\): half shoulder width; \(d_s\): offset of the stroke plane relative to the body;
  • \(r_w\in[0,R]\): spanwise coordinate. To avoid confusion with the body yaw rate \(r\), this document writes the spanwise coordinate as \(r_w\).

The wing aerodynamic frame convention is: +X is the wing normal, +Y is the spanwise/feathering axis. The local centre of pressure is written as

\[ \boldsymbol x_{cp}^{A}= \begin{bmatrix}0&s\,r_{cp}&-c_{cp}\end{bmatrix}^{T}, \qquad \boldsymbol F^{A}= \begin{bmatrix}F_N&0&0\end{bmatrix}^{T}. \]

mujoco_adapter.py uses a fixed matrix to align the URDF wing-body frame with this aerodynamic frame, and mirrors it for the right wing.

docs.title: 3. Why the wing geometry parameters are these integrals
docs.text:
Let the actual local chord be \(c(r_w)\) and the mean chord be

\[ \bar c=\frac{1}{R}\int_0^R c(r_w)\,dr_w. \]

Introduce the dimensionless variables

\[ \hat r=\frac{r_w}{R},\qquad \hat c(\hat r)=\frac{c(R\hat r)}{\bar c}. \]

r00 to r33 are in fact chord-weighted radial moments:

\[ r_{kk}=\int_0^1\hat c(\hat r)\hat r^k\,d\hat r, \qquad k=0,1,2,3. \]

z_cp0 to z_cp2 are moments weighted by the chord squared:

\[ z_{cp,k}=\int_0^1\hat c^2(\hat r)\hat r^k\,d\hat r, \qquad k=0,1,2. \]

Why does the normal force use \(r_{kk}\) while the aerodynamic pitching moment uses \(z_{cp,k}\)? Because the strip area is \(c(r_w)dr_w\), and the distance from the centre of pressure to the leading edge is also proportional to \(c(r_w)\). Hence

\[ dF_N\propto c(r_w)dr_w,\qquad dM_{aero}\propto c^2(r_w)dr_w. \]

The current wing is a \(70\times20\ \mathrm{mm}\) rectangular wing, so \(\hat c=1\) and therefore

\[ r_{00}=1,\quad r_{11}=\frac12,\quad r_{22}=\frac13,\quad r_{33}=\frac14, \] \[ z_{cp,0}=1,\quad z_{cp,1}=\frac12,\quad z_{cp,2}=\frac13. \]

These are exactly the values in Wing.json. The other main parameters are

\[ R=0.07\ \mathrm m,\quad \bar c=0.02\ \mathrm m,\quad \rho=1.225\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}, \] \[ d_0=0.01395\ \mathrm m,\qquad d_s=0.0189913\ \mathrm m. \]

examples/notebooks/02_wing_parameters.ipynb generates these parameters from polygon cross-sections of the wing planform and Gauss–Legendre quadrature. Its pressure-moment formula also requires the feathering-axis/leading-edge definition to be consistent with the parameter integrals; if the planform has a non-negligible chordwise offset relative to that axis, the full pressure moment acquires an offset term that the code does not currently retain.

docs.title: 4. Construction of the local relative velocity
4.1 The key structural fact: velocity is an affine function of the spanwise coordinate
docs.text:
The velocity of a point on a rigid body satisfies

\[ \boldsymbol V(r_w)=\boldsymbol V_O+\boldsymbol\Omega\times\boldsymbol r(r_w). \]

The spanwise position \(\boldsymbol r(r_w)\) is linear in \(r_w\), so after projection onto the two aerodynamic directions of the wing it remains a first-order function. The code writes them as

\[ U_i(r_w)=U_{i1}r_w+U_{i0},\qquad U_o(r_w)=U_{o1}r_w+U_{o0}. \]

Here \(U_i\) is the main in-plane inflow component and \(U_o\) is the out-of-plane / normal inflow component. All body translation, body rotation, stroke motion, deviation motion and geometric offsets are ultimately collected into these four coefficients.

Writing \(S_x=\sin x,C_x=\cos x\), the complete expressions in the current code are

\[ \begin{aligned} U_{o1}={}&s(pC_\psi C_\Phi-\dot\Phi S_\psi) +qS_\psi+rC_\psi S_\Phi+\dot\phi,\\ U_{o0}={}&s[-(u+qd_s)C_\phi S_\Phi -rd_0S_\phi S_\psi C_\Phi -(v-pd_s)S_\phi C_\psi\\ &\qquad+wS_\phi S_\psi S_\Phi +pd_0C_\phi C_\Phi] +(u+qd_s)S_\phi S_\psi C_\Phi\\ &\qquad+rd_0C_\phi S_\Phi+wC_\phi C_\Phi +pd_0S_\phi S_\psi S_\Phi,\\ U_{i1}={}&s[pS_\phi S_\psi C_\Phi+rC_\phi C_\Phi +\dot\Phi S_\phi C_\psi] -pC_\phi S_\Phi-qS_\phi C_\psi\\ &\qquad+rS_\phi S_\psi S_\Phi+\dot\psi C_\phi,\\ U_{i0}={}&s[rd_0C_\psi C_\Phi-(v-pd_s)S_\psi-wC_\psi S_\Phi] -(u+qd_s)C_\psi C_\Phi-pd_0C_\psi S_\Phi. \end{aligned} \]

With the defaults \(\phi=\Phi=\dot\phi=\dot\Phi=0\) they reduce to

\[ \begin{aligned} U_{o1}&=spC_\psi+qS_\psi, & U_{o0}&=spd_0+w,\\ U_{i1}&=sr+\dot\psi, & U_{i0}&=s[rd_0C_\psi-(v-pd_s)S_\psi]-(u+qd_s)C_\psi. \end{aligned} \]

If the body is completely stationary, one further obtains

\[ U_i(r_w)=\dot\psi r_w,\qquad U_o(r_w)=0, \]

which gives the standard result that the flapping velocity increases linearly with spanwise radius.

docs.title: 4.2 Why a fixed spanwise representative point is used
docs.text:
The code defines

\[ r_{cp}=R\frac{r_{33}}{r_{22}}. \]

The proof is as follows: for pure rotational flapping \(U^2\propto r_w^2\), and the force distribution satisfies

\[ dF\propto c(r_w)r_w^2dr_w. \]

So the spanwise centre of pressure for this case is

\[ \frac{\int_0^Rr_w c(r_w)r_w^2dr_w} {\int_0^Rc(r_w)r_w^2dr_w} =R\frac{r_{33}}{r_{22}}. \]

For a rectangular wing \(r_{cp}=3R/4=0.0525\ \mathrm m\). The code uses this fixed representative point to compute the angle of attack in all operating conditions. When \(U_{i0},U_{o0}\) are large the true centre of the resultant force generally moves; the current implementation does not update the spanwise CoP dynamically, which is one of the quasi-steady reduced-order assumptions.

docs.title: 5. Angle of attack, normal-force coefficient and centre-of-pressure fits
docs.text:
At the fixed representative point compute

\[ U_i^*=U_{i1}r_{cp}+U_{i0},\qquad U_o^*=U_{o1}r_{cp}+U_{o0}. \]

The flow-correction angle and the angle of attack are

\[ \delta_\alpha=\arctan\!\left(\frac{U_o^*}{U_i^*}\right), \] \[ \alpha=\theta+\operatorname{sgn}(U_i^*)\frac{\pi}{2}-\delta_\alpha. \]

When \(|U_i^*|\le10^{-12}\) the code sets \(\delta_\alpha=0\) directly instead of calling atan2. Near stroke reversal this angle definition therefore contains an artificial branch.

The normal-force coefficient is an empirical fit:

\[ C_N(\alpha)=1.8\sin(2\alpha)\cos\alpha +1.95\sin\alpha -1.5\cos(2\alpha)\sin\alpha. \]

The chordwise centre of pressure as a fraction of the local chord is

\[ d_{cp}(\alpha)=0.46-0.332\cos\alpha -0.037\cos(3\alpha)-0.013\cos(5\alpha). \]

These two expressions are empirical relations supplied as model inputs; they cannot be derived from first principles using the kinematics in the code. What can be verified rigorously are their structural properties:

\[ C_N(-\alpha)=-C_N(\alpha),\qquad d_{cp}(-\alpha)=d_{cp}(\alpha). \]

That is, reversing the angle of attack reverses the normal-force coefficient, while the centre-of-pressure fraction stays the same.

docs.title: 6. Closed-form normal force from the strip integral
docs.text:
The local velocity squared is

\[ U^2(r_w)=U_i^2(r_w)+U_o^2(r_w). \]

Substituting the two first-order functions and expanding:

\[ U^2(r_w)=a_{U2}r_w^2+a_{U1}r_w+a_{U0}, \]

where

\[ \begin{aligned} a_{U2}&=U_{i1}^2+U_{o1}^2,\\ a_{U1}&=2(U_{i1}U_{i0}+U_{o1}U_{o0}),\\ a_{U0}&=U_{i0}^2+U_{o0}^2. \end{aligned} \]

The quasi-steady strip normal force is

\[ dF_N=\frac12\rho C_N(\alpha)c(r_w)U^2(r_w)dr_w. \]

The model uses the angle of attack at the representative point, i.e. it assumes the whole wing shares one \(C_N\) at any instant. Therefore

\[ \begin{aligned} F_N &=\frac12\rho C_N\int_0^Rc(r_w) (a_{U2}r_w^2+a_{U1}r_w+a_{U0})dr_w\\ &=\frac12\rho\bar c C_N \left(a_{U2}R^3r_{22}+a_{U1}R^2r_{11}+a_{U0}Rr_{00}\right). \end{aligned} \]

This is force_raw. It is then multiplied by lift_scale and clipped to

\[ F_N^{clip}=\operatorname{clip}(F_N,-F_{max},F_{max}), \]

where the Python default is \(F_{max}=5\ \mathrm N\).

For a stationary body and pure flapping \(U=|\dot\psi|r_w\), so

\[ F_N=\frac12\rho\bar c C_N\dot\psi^2R^3r_{22}. \]

At the same stroke phase and amplitude \(\dot\psi\propto f\), hence

\[ F_N\propto f^2. \]

This is also the theoretical basis for the cycle-averaged model's use of \(L=k_f f^2\) later on; its coefficient still has to be identified with the full model, because passive feathering makes \(C_N\) vary over the cycle.

docs.title: 7. Aerodynamic pitching moment, chordwise CoP and rotational damping
7.1 Aerodynamic pitching moment produced by the pressure
docs.text:
The local pressure acts at a distance of approximately \(d_{cp}c(r_w)\) from the reference edge. The strip moment is therefore

\[ dM_{aero}=-d_{cp}(\alpha)c(r_w)dF_N. \]

Integrating gives

\[ M_{aero}=-\frac12\rho\bar c^2C_Nd_{cp} \left(a_{U2}R^3z_{cp,2} +a_{U1}R^2z_{cp,1} +a_{U0}Rz_{cp,0}\right). \]

The code then multiplies by moment_scale. Note that M_aero is not written into MuJoCo independently; it is converted into an equivalent chordwise centre of pressure:

\[ c_{cp}=-\frac{M_{aero}}{F_N^{raw}}. \]

As long as the force clip is not triggered,

\[ -c_{cp}F_N=M_{aero}, \]

so the \(y\)-axis moment produced in local coordinates by the force at the centre of pressure equals M_aero exactly. If \(F_N^{raw}=0\) the code sets \(c_{cp}=0\).

docs.title: 7.2 Feathering rotational damping
docs.text:
The implementation uses

\[ M_{rd}^{raw} =-\frac18\rho|\dot\theta|\dot\theta \left(5R\bar c^4z_{rd}\right). \]

It is then multiplied by moment_scale and clipped to \(\pm0.05\ \mathrm{N\,m}\). Its dissipativity can be shown directly:

\[ P_{rd}=M_{rd}\dot\theta =-K|\dot\theta|\dot\theta^2\le0, \qquad K\ge0. \]

Hence this term never actively injects energy into the feathering degree of freedom. For the current rectangular wing \(z_{rd}=1\).

docs.title: 7.3 From \(M_{aero}\), the CoP and \(M_{rd}\) to the complete single-wing wrench
docs.text:
This is the part where the quantities are most easily confused. First distinguish what each of them changes:

Quantity Changes the magnitude of the resultant force? Changes the point of application? Adds an independent moment? \(F_N\) yes no no \(M_{aero}\) no yes, through \(c_{cp}\) not applied directly \(r_{cp}\), \(c_{cp}\) no yes indirectly, through the lever arm \(M_{rd}\) no no yes

Therefore neither \(M_{aero}\) nor \(M_{rd}\) generates an additional share of lift. A single wing always has exactly one local normal force

\[ \boldsymbol F_A= \begin{bmatrix}F_N&0&0\end{bmatrix}^{T}. \]

The role of \(M_{aero}\) is to decide where along the chord this force is applied; \(M_{rd}\) adds a pure moment about the feathering axis. The computation can be written as

\[ \boxed{ (F_N,M_{aero},M_{rd}) \longrightarrow (r_{cp},c_{cp}) \longrightarrow (\boldsymbol F_A,\boldsymbol r_{cp,A}) \longrightarrow (\boldsymbol F_W,\boldsymbol\tau_W) }. \]

For wing \(k\), \(k\in\{L,R\}\), let \(s_L=+1\) and \(s_R=-1\). The position of the centre of pressure relative to the wing-body frame origin is

\[ \boldsymbol r_{cp,A,k} = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ s_k r_{cp}\\ -c_{cp,k} \end{bmatrix}. \]

But external torques in MuJoCo must be taken about the centre of mass of that wing. Define the position of the wing centre of mass relative to the wing-body origin

\[ \boldsymbol r_{com,A,k} =R_{WA,k}^{T} \left( \boldsymbol x_{com,W,k}-\boldsymbol x_{body,W,k} \right), \]

then the true lever arm from the centre of mass to the centre of pressure is

\[ \boldsymbol\ell_{A,k} =\boldsymbol r_{cp,A,k}-\boldsymbol r_{com,A,k} = \begin{bmatrix} \ell_x&\ell_y&\ell_z \end{bmatrix}^{T}. \]

The cross product with the local force can be fully expanded:

\[ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol\tau_{F,A,k} &=\boldsymbol\ell_{A,k}\times\boldsymbol F_{A,k}\\ &= \begin{bmatrix} \ell_x\\ \ell_y\\ \ell_z \end{bmatrix} \times \begin{bmatrix} F_{N,k}\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\\ &= \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ \ell_zF_{N,k}\\ -\ell_yF_{N,k} \end{bmatrix}. \end{aligned} \]

This result says:

  1. the chordwise lever arm \(\ell_z\) produces a local \(y\)-axis pitching moment;
  2. the spanwise lever arm \(\ell_y\) produces a local \(z\)-axis moment;
  3. the local normal force alone does not produce a local \(x\)-axis moment through this lever arm.

If one temporarily ignores the chordwise offset between the wing-body origin and the centre of mass, i.e. takes

\[ \ell_z=-c_{cp,k}, \]

then

\[ \tau_{F,A,k,y} =-c_{cp,k}F_{N,k} =M_{aero,k}. \]

This is the rigorous meaning of "implementing \(M_{aero}\) implicitly through the CoP". If the wing-body origin and the centre of mass do not coincide, then

\[ \ell_z=-c_{cp,k}-r_{com,A,k,z}, \]

so the \(y\)-axis moment about the centre of mass additionally contains

\[ -r_{com,A,k,z}F_{N,k}, \]

which is the moment that necessarily appears when the reference point is moved from the wing-body origin to the centre of mass; it is not a double count of the aerodynamic pitching moment.

The rotational damping is a pure moment independent of the centre-of-pressure lever arm:

\[ \boldsymbol\tau_{rd,A,k} = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ M_{rd,k}\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Hence the total local moment on one wing is

\[ \boldsymbol\tau_{A,k} =\boldsymbol\tau_{F,A,k} +\boldsymbol\tau_{rd,A,k} = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ \ell_zF_{N,k}+M_{rd,k}\\ -\ell_yF_{N,k} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Using the fact that rotation matrices preserve the cross product,

\[ R(\boldsymbol a\times\boldsymbol b) =(R\boldsymbol a)\times(R\boldsymbol b), \]

the single-wing wrench can be rotated into the world frame:

\[ \boldsymbol F_{W,k}=R_{WA,k}\boldsymbol F_{A,k}, \qquad \boldsymbol\tau_{W,k}=R_{WA,k}\boldsymbol\tau_{A,k}. \]

This is exactly equivalent to the code's approach of first computing the world-frame CoP and then taking the cross product in the world frame.

docs.title: 7.4 From the left and right single wings to \(F_{\mathrm{lift,total}}\)
docs.text:
The world-frame resultant given by the pure aerodynamic functions for the left and right wings is a vector sum, not a sum of absolute values:

\[ \boldsymbol F_{\mathrm{pure,total}} =\boldsymbol F_{W,L}+\boldsymbol F_{W,R} =R_{WA,L} \begin{bmatrix}F_{N,L}\\0\\0\end{bmatrix} +R_{WA,R} \begin{bmatrix}F_{N,R}\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}. \]

If world \(+z\) is defined as vertically upward, the true instantaneous total lift is

\[ F_{\mathrm{lift,total}}^{W} =\boldsymbol e_z^{T}\boldsymbol F_{\mathrm{applied,total}} =F_{\mathrm{applied,total},z}. \]

Because of the STL normal convention the current adapter flips the forces of both wings, so

\[ \boldsymbol F_{\mathrm{applied},k}=-\boldsymbol F_{W,k}, \]

and hence

\[ \boldsymbol F_{\mathrm{applied,total}} =-\left(\boldsymbol F_{W,L}+\boldsymbol F_{W,R}\right) =-\boldsymbol F_{\mathrm{pure,total}}. \]

This is exactly the value the adapter finally stores in the diagnostic quantity \(F_{\mathrm{world}}\). Therefore, in the current model, the actual vertical aerodynamic force on the robot should be judged with

\[ \boxed{ F_{\mathrm{lift,total}}^{W} =\text{diagnostics}[F_{\mathrm{world}}]_z }. \]

The scalar in the code

\[ \text{lift\_total}=|F_{N,L}|+|F_{N,R}| \]

has a different meaning. It merely adds the magnitudes of the normal forces in the two wing aerodynamic frames. It does not contain the following information:

  1. the inclination of the wing normal relative to the world vertical;
  2. whether the horizontal components of the left and right wings cancel or add;
  3. the global flip the adapter applies for the STL normal;
  4. any moment produced by \(M_{aero}\), the CoP and \(M_{rd}\).

Let the world-frame vertical projection of each wing's actual normal be

\[ \gamma_k =\boldsymbol e_z^{T}R_{WA,k} \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}, \]

then the actual total vertical aerodynamic force can be written explicitly as

\[ F_{\mathrm{lift,total}}^{W} =-\gamma_LF_{N,L}-\gamma_RF_{N,R}. \]

Only when both wing normals are aligned with the vertical and the sign conventions have been unified can it be approximated as

\[ F_{\mathrm{lift,total}}^{W} \approx |F_{N,L}|+|F_{N,R}|. \]

So the \(\text{lift\_total}\) in the code is better used as an "aerodynamic load intensity" diagnostic; it cannot be treated directly as world-frame lift at arbitrary attitude.

An interface-level numerical check also confirmed this relationship: at every step the vector sum of the left and right xfrc_applied[:, :3] equals the adapter's final diagnostics["F_world"] exactly; the norm of the difference in the current check is 0.

docs.title: 7.5 How the total moment of the left and right wings is defined
docs.text:
The moments of the two wings cannot simply be added at arbitrary reference points. The moment the code writes for each wing is about that wing's centre of mass. To obtain the total aerodynamic moment of the whole robot about a robot reference point \(O\), use

\[ \boldsymbol\tau_{O,\mathrm{total}} =\sum_{k\in\{L,R\}} \left[ \boldsymbol\tau_{\mathrm{applied},k} +(\boldsymbol x_{com,W,k}-\boldsymbol x_{O,W}) \times\boldsymbol F_{\mathrm{applied},k} \right]. \]

The current adapter keeps the moment computed by the pure function and flips only the force:

\[ \boldsymbol\tau_{\mathrm{applied},k} =\boldsymbol\tau_{W,k}, \qquad \boldsymbol F_{\mathrm{applied},k} =-\boldsymbol F_{W,k}. \]

Hence the actual wrench after the adapter must be understood directly in terms of the two quantities above; it can no longer be assumed equivalent to "the flipped force still acting at the original CoP". MuJoCo writes the left and right wrenches into the corresponding wing bodies and transmits them through the joint constraints as generalised forces on the whole robot.

docs.title: 8. From the local force to the MuJoCo world-frame wrench
docs.text:
Let \(R_{WA}\) be the rotation matrix from the wing aerodynamic frame to the world frame. The pure function world_wrench computes

\[ \boldsymbol x_{cp}^{W}=\boldsymbol x_{body}^{W} +R_{WA}\boldsymbol x_{cp}^{A}, \] \[ \boldsymbol F^{W}=R_{WA}\boldsymbol F^{A}, \] \[ \boldsymbol\tau_F^{W}= (\boldsymbol x_{cp}^{W}-\boldsymbol x_{com}^{W})\times\boldsymbol F^{W}, \] \[ \boldsymbol\tau_{rd}^{W}=R_{WA} \begin{bmatrix}0&M_{rd}&0\end{bmatrix}^{T}, \qquad \boldsymbol\tau^{W}=\boldsymbol\tau_F^{W}+\boldsymbol\tau_{rd}^{W}. \]

The final wrench ordering follows MuJoCo:

\[ \boldsymbol w= [F_x,F_y,F_z,\tau_x,\tau_y,\tau_z]^T. \]

With read_only=True all diagnostics are computed as usual, but the wrench returned for xfrc_applied is zero.

docs.title: 8.1 The adapter's actual normal correction
docs.text:
The STL wing normal is opposite to the oriented normal of the aerodynamic model. After world_wrench has finished, MuJoCoAeroAdapter performs

\[ \boldsymbol F_{applied}=-\boldsymbol F_{pure},\qquad \boldsymbol\tau_{applied}=\boldsymbol\tau_{pure}. \]

That is, only the first three force components are flipped; the r×F moment already computed from the original force is not flipped, nor is the damping moment. This behaviour was intentional for the current URDF/STL coordinate convention, but it means the wrench the adapter finally injects is no longer strictly equivalent to "applying the flipped force at the same CoP". F_world in the diagnostics is also flipped to match the force actually applied. [Translator's note: this force flip was removed on 2026-10-28; see quasi_steady_model.md.]

docs.title: 9. Left/right wing handling and symmetry
docs.text:
aero_step uses \(s=+1\) for the left wing and \(s=-1\) for the right wing. The adapter also applies stroke_sign=-1 to the right-wing stroke angle and rate, to bring the mirrored URDF joint into the common aerodynamic sign convention. The sign of the feathering angle is set by pitch_axis_y; the current adapter passes \(+1\).

In the ideal mirrored state the normal forces of the two wings may have opposite signs in their own local frames, but after the mirrored rotation and the adapter's normal correction the vertical components add while the lateral components and part of the moments cancel. The code diagnostic

\[ \texttt{lift\_total}=|F_{N,L}|+|F_{N,R}| \]

is only the sum of the absolute local normal forces, not the strict world-frame vertical lift; the actual world resultant should be read from diagnostics["F_world"].

docs.title: 10. Cycle-averaged hover model
docs.text: Free flight with fix=False does not use the per-wing instantaneous model above but AveragedHoverAero (now flapsim/aero/cycle_averaged.py). At the same time the environment treats the robot dynamics as a single rigid body of mass \(m=0.03\ \mathrm{kg}\); the sub-bodies retain only tiny numerical inertias, and the stroke-joint velocities do not take part in dynamic energy injection.

docs.title: 10.1 Mean lift
docs.text:
The model is written as

\[ L(f)=k_f f^2, \qquad k_f=\frac{0.14858349039827917}{30^2} =1.6509276711\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N/Hz^2}. \]

The body-frame thrust direction is set by the plate command:

\[ \boldsymbol n_B= \frac{[-\delta_r,-\delta_p,1]^T} {\sqrt{1+\delta_r^2+\delta_p^2}}, \qquad \boldsymbol F_{thrust}^{W}=R_{WB}L\boldsymbol n_B. \]

where \(\delta_p=\texttt{pitch\_joint}\) and \(\delta_r=\texttt{roll\_joint}\). For small angles

\[ \boldsymbol n_B\approx[-\delta_r,-\delta_p,1]^T, \]

so tilting the plate produces horizontal thrust linearly.

The world-frame horizontal damping is

\[ \boldsymbol F_{xy}^{W}\leftarrow \boldsymbol F_{xy}^{W}-k_v\boldsymbol v_{xy}^{W}, \qquad k_v=0.06\ \mathrm{N\,s/m}. \]

docs.title: 10.2 Mean control moments
docs.text:
The identified moments scale with the square of frequency:

\[ \lambda_f=\left(\frac{f}{42}\right)^2. \]

The body-frame moment is

\[ \boldsymbol\tau_B= \lambda_f \begin{bmatrix} k_{roll}\delta_p\\ -k_{pitch}\delta_r\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} -D_\omega\boldsymbol\omega_B, \]

where

\[ k_{roll}=\frac{0.01055}{20},\quad k_{pitch}=\frac{0.01144}{20}\quad[\mathrm{N\,m/rad}], \] \[ D_\omega=\operatorname{diag}(2,2,1)\times10^{-4} \quad[\mathrm{N\,m\,s/rad}]. \]

The URDF naming and the physical axes are crossed: pitch_joint mainly controls the roll moment and roll_joint mainly controls the pitch moment. The expression above therefore contains cross terms, rather than each named angle controlling the axis of the same name.

docs.title: 10.3 Consistency of the hover frequency
docs.text:
The weight of the 30 g equivalent mass is

\[ mg=0.03\times9.81=0.2943\ \mathrm N. \]

From \(k_f f_h^2=mg\),

\[ f_h=\sqrt{\frac{mg}{k_f}}=42.2213\ \mathrm{Hz}. \]

This agrees with the nominal hover_frequency=42 Hz of HoveringController (now flapsim/controllers/hover_pid.py). At 42 Hz the model lift is \(0.291224\ \mathrm N\), about \(1.05\%\) below the weight; the remaining steady-state error is compensated by the frequency correction of the altitude PID.

docs.title: 11. Numerical validation
docs.text: The following checks were run on the repository code and the Wing.json current at the time of writing; all units are SI.

docs.title: 11.1 Closed-form integral check of the pure functions
docs.text:
Choose the representative state

\[ \psi=0.37,\ \dot\psi=92,\ \theta=0.48,\ \dot\theta=-11, \] \[ \boldsymbol v_B=(0.3,-0.2,0.1),\quad \boldsymbol\omega_B=(0.7,-0.5,0.4). \]

Integrate the strip formula numerically with 200001 spanwise points and compare with the closed-form geometric-moment formula in wing_aero:

Check Closed form (code) Numerical integration Relative error \(F_N\) 0.0351425732167 N 0.0351425732172 N \(1.36\times10^{-11}\) \(M_{aero}\) -0.000406734027976 N·m -0.000406734027981 N·m \(1.36\times10^{-11}\)

Conclusion: the closed-form integration from the affine velocity expansion to the rxx/z_cpx geometric moments is implemented correctly; the error comes only from the numerical quadrature.

Other algebraic properties verified:

Property Result \(r_{cp}=3R/4\) 0.05250000000000003 m \(-M_{aero}/F_N=c_{cp}\) both sides 0.0115738260106 m \(M_{rd}\dot\theta\) \(-1.14133\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm W<0\) Force ratio at equal phase, 15 Hz to 30 Hz 4.0 Maximum residual of \(C_N\) oddness (1001 points) 0.0 Maximum residual of \(d_{cp}\) evenness (1001 points) 0.0

docs.title: 11.2 Full fixed-base simulation frequency sweep
docs.text:
Set 20, 30 and 40 Hz respectively, run for 0.6 s, discard the first 0.3 s, and average the adapter's actual world-frame vertical force:

Frequency Mean \(F_z\) \(F_z/f^2\) 20 Hz 0.0661819985 N \(1.65455\times10^{-4}\) N/Hz² 30 Hz 0.1486352297 N \(1.65150\times10^{-4}\) N/Hz² 40 Hz 0.2639114107 N \(1.64945\times10^{-4}\) N/Hz²

The 30 Hz result differs from the identification point \(0.1485834904\ \mathrm N\) used by the averaged model by about \(0.035\%\). \(F_z/f^2\) is essentially constant over the three points, showing that the reduction \(L=k_ff^2\) is a reasonable local approximation in the current passive-feathering steady state.

docs.title: 11.3 Free hover check
docs.text:
Start the free model from \(z=0.5\ \mathrm m\) and simulate for 2.5 s:

Metric Result Final altitude 0.479012 m Altitude range 0.470056–0.500000 m Mean altitude over the last 0.5 s 0.475627 m Mean frequency over the last 0.5 s 42.234855 Hz

Conclusion: the averaged model stays bounded and converges near the nominal hover frequency; within the finite time there is still an altitude offset of about 2.4 cm, so this result demonstrates qualitative stability and order-of-magnitude consistency of model and controller, and should not be read as strict zero steady-state error or as validation over the full flight envelope.

docs.title: 12. What has been proven, model assumptions and implementation boundaries
12.1 What can be proven rigorously from the implementation or re-checked numerically
docs.text:
1. Rigid-body kinematics make the two local velocity components first-order functions of the spanwise coordinate;
  2. the velocity squared is therefore a quadratic polynomial, and the spanwise integral can be completed exactly with precomputed geometric moments;
  3. without clipping, the moment produced by the chordwise CoP is algebraically equivalent to M_aero;
  4. the rotational damping always satisfies \(M_{rd}\dot\theta\le0\);
  5. the pure-flapping normal force at equal phase scales with \(f^2\); the current full fixed-base sweep also supports this approximation;
  6. the nominal hover frequency of the cycle-averaged model is consistent with balancing the 30 g weight.

docs.title: 12.2 What cannot be called a first-principles proof
docs.text:
1. \(C_N(\alpha)\) and \(d_{cp}(\alpha)\) are empirical fits whose accuracy needs experimental or higher-fidelity CFD data;
  2. replacing the spanwise-varying angle of attack by the angle at a single representative point is a quasi-steady reduced-order assumption;
  3. the fixed \(r_{cp}=Rr_{33}/r_{22}\) is strictly valid only when the velocity squared is dominated by the \(r_w^2\) term;
  4. the current model does not explicitly include wake capture, added mass, wing–wing interaction, dynamic stall or ground effect;
  5. the cycle-averaged model is identified only at a finite set of operating points and cannot automatically be extrapolated to arbitrary amplitude, frequency, attitude or high-speed flight.

docs.title: 12.3 Boundaries to watch when reading and modifying the code
docs.text:
1. Although Wing.json carries an options block, the current MuJoCoAeroAdapter constructs AeroOptions() directly and does not load the options from the JSON. Hence the force_limit=2.0 in the JSON has no effect; the actual default is the 5.0 N in the Python dataclass.
  2. force_raw is clipped but M_aero is not, and chord_CoP is computed from the unclipped force_raw. Once the force clip triggers, r×F_clipped no longer equals the original M_aero.
  3. The adapter flips only the final force, not the already computed moment; the pure-function wrench and the wrench actually injected into MuJoCo must therefore be distinguished.
  4. The angle of attack uses atan(U_o/U_i) and forces the correction angle to zero when \(U_i\approx0\); near stroke reversal it lacks the full quadrant continuity of atan2.
  5. diagnostics["lift_total"] is the sum of the absolute local normal forces of the two wings; hover should be judged with the world-frame F_world[2], and lift_total must not be taken directly as vertical lift.
  6. fix=True/False does not only fix or free the root; it also switches the aerodynamic model and the way the whole-robot mass/inertia is modelled. This model change must be taken into account when comparing the two simulations.

docs.title: 13. Summary
docs.text:
The core of the current per-wing aero can be summarised as

\[ \boxed{ \text{rigid-body kinematics} \Rightarrow U_i,U_o\text{ are first-order in }r_w \Rightarrow U^2\text{ is quadratic} \Rightarrow \text{closed-form }F_N,M_{aero}\text{ from the wing geometric moments} \Rightarrow \text{CoP + wrench written to MuJoCo} } \]

The cycle-averaged model further reduces the full periodic response above to

\[ \boxed{L=k_ff^2+\text{tilt direction}+\text{linear damping}+\text{identified control moments}} \]

The closed-form integration, the centre-of-pressure identity, the dissipativity of the damping and the frequency-squared law have all been verified algebraically or numerically. The main uncertainty of the model lies not in the integration implementation but in the empirical aerodynamic coefficients, the single-point angle of attack, the fixed spanwise centre of pressure, and the range over which the fixed-base identification extrapolates to free flight.

docs.title: Quasi-steady blade-element model: conventions and equations
docs.text: This page states the conventions FlapSim uses for wings and summarises the quasi-steady model implemented in flapsim/fluid/aero.py. The complete derivation with closed-form integrals is in the Chinese original, docs/zh/derivations/quasi_steady_aero.md; an English translation is planned.

docs.title: Wing aero frame
docs.text:
Every wing has an aerodynamic frame attached to its MuJoCo body:

Axis Meaning +Y feathering axis, side * span where span points root to tip -Z chord direction from the leading-edge hinge to the trailing edge +X surface normal, X = Y x Z

A manifest gives span and chord; the normal is derived. side is +1 for a left wing and -1 for its mirror image, so mirrored wings share one frame orientation at the neutral pose and the side factor inside the formulas places the centre of pressure on each wing. Positive stroke angle psi is a right-handed rotation about side * Z; positive feathering angle theta is a right-handed rotation about +Y for both wings. The manifest's joint sign fields convert MuJoCo joint coordinates into these conventions, and flapsim.robot.load checks them at the neutral pose and warns when a sign or the chord direction looks reversed.

docs.title: Equations
docs.text:
With body velocities (u, v, w) and rates (p, q, r) expressed in the torso frame, the relative flow at span coordinate r_w has a component U_i along +X and U_o along +Z, both affine in r_w:

U_i(r_w) = U_i1 r_w + U_i0,     U_o(r_w) = U_o1 r_w + U_o0

(the coefficients are the long expressions in wing_aero). The angle of attack is evaluated at the fixed spanwise centre of pressure r_cp = R r33 / r22:

alpha = theta + sign(U_i*) pi/2 - atan(U_o* / U_i*)
C_N(alpha) = 1.8 sin(2 alpha) cos(alpha) + 1.95 sin(alpha) - 1.5 cos(2 alpha) sin(alpha)
d_cp(alpha) = 0.46 - 0.332 cos(alpha) - 0.037 cos(3 alpha) - 0.013 cos(5 alpha)

C_N is odd in alpha, so the normal force carries the sign of the flow; d_cp is even. With U^2 = a_U2 r_w^2 + a_U1 r_w + a_U0 the closed-form blade-element integrals give

F_N    =  1/2 rho c C_N (a_U2 R^3 r22 + a_U1 R^2 r11 + a_U0 R r00)
M_aero = -1/2 rho c^2 C_N d_cp (a_U2 R^3 z_cp2 + a_U1 R^2 z_cp1 + a_U0 R z_cp0)
M_rd   = -1/8 rho |theta_dot| theta_dot (5 R c^4 z_rd)

where r_kk and z_cpk are the planform integrals from flapsim.wings.planform. M_aero is not applied as a separate torque: it is converted into the chordwise centre of pressure chord_CoP = -M_aero / F_N (always positive), and the single force F_N along +X is applied at [0, side * span_CoP, -chord_CoP]. The torque about the body centre of mass is r x F plus the rotational damping M_rd about +Y. The torque on the feathering hinge therefore always turns the trailing edge downstream, which is what makes passive feathering work.

docs.title: Hinge geometry
docs.text: The feathering axis need not coincide with the leading edge. planform. pitch_axis_fraction places the hinge inside the chord at that fraction from the leading edge; planform.leading_edge_offset places the leading edge that many metres beyond the hinge (a root spar). Both shift the chordwise centre of pressure, chord_CoP = x_le + (d_cp - x0) c_eff, and the rotational damping integral z_rd, which grows with the fourth power of the distance from the hinge.

docs.title: Passive feathering and the wing mass model
docs.text: Passive feathering is a driven oscillator: the aerodynamic moment turns the trailing edge downstream, rotational damping and the hinge spring resist, and the wing's inertia, including the inertial torque from the stroke acceleration acting on a centre of mass offset from the hinge, carries the motion through reversal. When inertia dominates, the response is in anti-phase with the moment: the trailing edge leads, the angle of attack is inverted and the mean lift is negative. CAD meshes exported as uniform solids often put the wing centroid far behind the hinge and produce exactly this. A membrane wing carries most of its mass in the leading-edge spar, so manifests should declare the mass distribution explicitly with wings[].mass_model (spar_plate with a spar fraction, thin_plate, or explicit values in wing coordinates). The example robot uses spar_plate with 80 percent of 62.6 mg in the spar; with the URDF's own centroid, 22 mm aft, it does not fly.

docs.title: Correction relative to the pre-platform implementation
docs.text: The earlier implementation multiplied M_aero by sign(alpha). Since C_N is odd, that made M_aero = -|...| independent of the flow direction, so the centre of pressure switched to the opposite side of the hinge at every stroke reversal and the force and torque were no longer those of one force acting at one point. A translational force flip in the MuJoCo adapter compensated the resulting lift sign for the example robot, at the cost of an inconsistent force/torque pair. On 2026-10-28 the moment was restored to -d_cp c F_N as written in the derivation, the flip was removed, and the wing frame was redefined through span and chord so the side of the hinge on which the plate lies is explicit. The regression values in tests/test_lift_sweep.py were re-measured after this change.

docs.title: Record of the aerodynamic force direction bug fix
docs.text: Translated from the Chinese original (docs/zh/notes/aero_force_sign_fix.md). It documents the implementation as it stood before 2026-10-28; the pitching-moment sign and the removed force flip are described in quasi_steady_model.md.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text:
With base_link fixed, raising the flapping frequency clearly increased the absolute normal force of the left and right wings, yet the mean world-frame Fz was always negative:

20 Hz: -0.067 mN
30 Hz: -0.300 mN
40 Hz: -0.823 mN
50 Hz: -1.685 mN
60 Hz: -2.774 mN

This means that the higher the frequency, the larger the mean downward aerodynamic force on the robot. The hovering controller kept raising the frequency as the altitude dropped, forming a wrong positive feedback loop.

Note: the sum of the left and right |F_N| exceeding the robot's weight does not mean that enough world-frame +Z lift is produced. The transformed mean F_world[2] must be checked.

docs.title: Comparison with FlapX
docs.text:
Running the FlapX Purdue Flapper in the parent directory directly, with

frequency = 30 Hz
amplitude = 1.5 rad
fluid = aero
torso = clamped

gives

L_stroke / R_stroke correlation = 1.0
L_pitch  / R_pitch  correlation = 1.0
mean Fz = +0.1029 N

The FlapX joint axes are:

L_stroke: +Z
R_stroke: -Z
L_pitch:  +Y
R_pitch:  +Y

The left and right stroke actuators receive the same position command, and the mirrored motion is realised by opposite joint axes. The left and right passive-pitch joint coordinates have the same sign.

docs.title: 1. Stroke joint coordinate
docs.text:
After the joint-origin rotation in the current URDF, the world axes of both strokes are close to +Z. FlapSim must therefore use opposite joint coordinates to obtain a mirrored stroke:

q_right_stroke = -q_left_stroke

Before being passed into the FlapX aerodynamic formulas, the right-wing stroke coordinate is converted back to the common aerodynamic convention through stroke_sign=-1.

docs.title: 2. Wrong right-wing pitch sign
docs.text:
The adapter once contained an experimental

pitch_sign = -1.0

But in the FlapX Purdue model both pitch axes are +Y, so the left and right pitch coordinates should use the same sign. That sign inversion has been removed.

docs.title: 3. Inconsistent neutral aero frames of the left and right wings
docs.text:
In FlapX, the rotation matrices of L_wing and R_wing at the neutral pose are both the identity, i.e. the left and right aero frames coincide exactly.

After URDF import, the left and right wing bodies use different local mesh frames. If the same fixed body-to-aero transform is applied directly to both, the chord/normal of the right wing points in the wrong direction.

The fix is to calibrate at the model's neutral pose:

neutral_aero_rotation = left_body_rotation @ aero_from_body_left

aero_from_body_right = right_body_rotation.T @ neutral_aero_rotation

After calibration, the maximum matrix error between the left and right neutral aero frames is about

1.3e-15

docs.title: 4. STL normal opposite to the FlapX oriented normal
docs.text:
A phase-by-phase comparison of FlapX and FlapSim showed that the stroke and feathering phases already agreed, but the world Fz had exactly the opposite sign.

Example phase data:

FlapX:   +0.256, -0.052, +0.254, -0.051 ... N
FlapSim: -0.210, +0.201, -0.212, +0.200 ... N

This shows that the passive feathering phase is not inverted; rather, the oriented normal of the imported STL is opposite to the FlapX force convention.

The final treatment was to invert only the translational normal force applied to the wing body, in MuJoCoAeroAdapter.apply_forces():

left_wrench = result["xfrc_applied_L"].copy()
right_wrench = result["xfrc_applied_R"].copy()

left_wrench[:3] *= -1.0
right_wrench[:3] *= -1.0

The existing aerodynamic torque is left unchanged, because it already produces the correct reversal phase of passive feathering. Multiplying the whole wrench by -1 would also flip the feathering torque and destroy the passive-rotation dynamics that were already correct. [Translator's note: this force flip was removed on 2026-10-28 together with the pitching-moment sign correction; see quasi_steady_model.md.]

F_world in the diagnostics is inverted as well, so that the telemetry represents the force actually applied:

self.diagnostics["F_world"] = -np.asarray(result["diagnostics"]["F_world"])

docs.title: Feathering mirror constraint
docs.text:
The local frames of the left and right wing meshes in the URDF are not strict mirror images. A check of the spatial poses showed that the wing surfaces are mirror images in world coordinates only when the feathering joint coordinates have the same sign.

A passive joint equality was therefore added to the model:

q_left_feathering = q_right_feathering

This equality does not prescribe a feathering trajectory, and no feathering actuator was added. The angle is still determined by aerodynamic force, inertia, spring, damping and the joint limits.

docs.title: Mass and numerical parameters
docs.text:
The robot mass was redistributed as:

base_link + link1                         = 20 g
link2 + left/right arm + left/right wing = 10 g
total                                     = 30 g

The mass of each wing was reduced from about 4.4 g to 0.0626 g, with the inertia scaled in proportion to the mass. Otherwise the FlapX-scale aerodynamic moments cannot overcome the wing's gravitational moment and rotational inertia, and the feathering stays pinned at one limit for long periods.

The simulation uses:

timestep   = 5e-5 s
integrator = implicitfast

Passive feathering parameters:

range        = ±0.785398 rad
stiffness    = 2e-7 N·m/rad
damping      = 1e-9 N·m·s/rad
frictionloss = 1e-8 N·m
armature     = 1e-10 kg·m²

docs.title: Lift validation after the fix
docs.text:
Fixed-base frequency sweep at amplitude 1.5 rad:

20 Hz: mean Fz = +0.0662 N, L/W = 0.225
30 Hz: mean Fz = +0.1486 N, L/W = 0.505
40 Hz: mean Fz = +0.2638 N, L/W = 0.896
50 Hz: mean Fz = +0.4107 N, L/W = 1.396

[Translator's note: these are historical measurements from the pre-2026-10-28 implementation; the current regression values are in tests/test_lift_sweep.py.]

It now holds that:

frequency increases -> mean +Z lift increases

The weight of the 30 g robot is:

0.03 * 9.81 = 0.2943 N

From the sweep results the hover frequency is estimated at about 42 Hz.

docs.title: Subsequent state of the hovering controller
docs.text:
The sign of the aerodynamic force in the altitude direction has been fixed, and the floating-base model produces a mean lift close to the weight at about 42 Hz.

However, the attitude loop may still flip through large angles within 0.1--0.2 s. The remaining issues are:

  • the periodic aerodynamic moment fluctuates strongly at 42 Hz;
  • the attitude control uses instantaneous states directly, without low-pass filtering or averaging over a flap cycle;
  • the plate-to-body moment gain changes with frequency;
  • there is no independent yaw control channel yet;
  • Euler angles become singular near large attitudes.

So the aerodynamic force sign bug is fixed, but fully stable hovering still needs cycle-averaged attitude estimation, gain scheduling based on the actual control effectiveness, and a more reliable quaternion attitude controller.
